newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran no military threat in Gulf - Iranian expert.
newsitem.headline: Iran no military threat in Gulf - Iranian expert.

text.p: Iran poses no military threat to its oil-rich Gulf Arab neighbours and is building up its forces to defend itself against powers from outside the region, an Iranian foreign policy expert said on Wednesday.
"Iran is not at the stage at which it could be a real threat to this region," said Abbas Haghighat at Tehran's Institute for Political and International Studies (IPIS).

The United States, which has stepped up its naval presence in the Gulf since the 1990-91 Gulf crisis and has about 20,000 armed forces stationed in the region, has voiced concern over Iran's arms buildup after the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq war.

Iran is about to take delivery of a third Russian-made submarine, giving it additional firepower capable of striking shipping, including tankers which carry 15 million barrels of oil through the strategic waterway each day.
Iran has carried out extensive naval exercises which have included test firing of anti-ship cruise missiles.
"We feel a threat -- not from the region but from outside. This threat is from the foreign powers in the region. So we have to have enough capability for defending ourselves," Haghighat told Reuters.
"These (Iranian) naval exercises or other things you see in the Persian Gulf are because we feel threatened by outside powers...The (Arab) countries in the region are not a threat to Iran," he added.

IPIS is a research body that reports to Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati and although its views are not official, comments made by its experts are close to government thinking. Haghighat heads its Persian Gulf and Middle East Research Centre.
"The presence of foreign troops in the region is creating a crisis in the region. For example, the U.S. always mentions to the region 'Iran is a threat. Watch for Iran'," he said.
The United States has imposed unilateral trade sanctions against Iran as part of its "dual containment" policy against Iran and neighbouring Iraq.
Washington accuses Tehran of sponsoring international terrorism and seeking nuclear weapons. Tehran denies this.

Haghighat said Iran's Gulf Arab neighbours were buying arms from Western powers because of U.S. pressure and also because they felt a threat from Iraq and had continuing border disputes between themselves.
The most prominent of these is between the small Gulf states of Qatar and Bahrain which both claim sovereignty over a group of reefs and islands potentially rich in oil.
Haghighat said Gulf Arabs and Iran also had to work together to guarantee the security of the region.
"The security of the region should be maintained by countries in the region. Each country should have his share in the security of the region. In that case we have a stable region," he said.
